question.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial, we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(6,0.9),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.9)^{x}(0.1)^{6-x}.
$$

Computing $P(X<5)$ will require us to compute $f(x)$ at $x=0,1,2,3,4.$ However, if we compute the complement $P(X\ge 5)$ instead, then we will only have to compute $f(x)$ at $x=5,6,$ which will result in a much faster computation.

Computing $P(X\ge 5),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =P(X\in \{5,6\}) \\  & =f(5)+f(6) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5})(0.9)^{5}(0.1)^{6-5}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{6})(0.9)^{6}(0.1)^{6-6} \\  & =6(0.9)^{5}(0.1)+(0.9)^{6} \\  & ≈0.886\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =1-P(X\ge 5) \\  & ≈1-0.886 \\  & ≈0.114\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
